summaries.example: Imagine a ball rolling down a hill. Its path depends on the hill, the push, the wind, and other causes. Abner used a similar idea for human choices: he said each choice is shaped by earlier causes, even when it feels like we are choosing freely.
summaries.summary: Abner of Burgos lived in medieval Spain, probably from about 1260 to 1347. He first worked within Jewish philosophy, especially traditions connected with Aristotle and Maimonides. After many years of doubt, he converted to Christianity and became known as Alfonso of Valladolid. He then wrote books defending Christianity and challenging Jewish arguments. His writings were not only religious debates. They also explored difficult philosophical questions. Abner offered an unusual explanation of the Trinity and the Incarnation, claiming that divine reality is present throughout the world in different degrees. He also defended determinism: the view that everything happens through causes, including human decisions. In science, he questioned Aristotle’s ideas about place, motion, voids, and the connection between bodies and their qualities. Some of his books were lost, so scholars reconstruct parts of his scientific views from other writings. Abner influenced later Jewish debates, especially the work of Hasdai Crescas. His story also shows how philosophy, science, and religious debate were closely connected in medieval Spain.
key_ideas: Abner of Burgos was a Jewish philosopher and rabbi who later became a Christian and took the name Alfonso of Valladolid.
He wrote arguments about Judaism and Christianity, including the Trinity and the Incarnation.
He argued that human choices are caused by earlier events, so true free choice does not exist.
He criticized parts of Aristotle’s science, especially ideas about space, motion, and matter.
His ideas influenced the Jewish philosopher Hasdai Crescas and, through Crescas, later Western philosophy.
summaries.why_it_matters: Abner matters because he crossed several intellectual boundaries: Jewish and Christian communities, religious debate and philosophy, and theology and science. His arguments helped later thinkers examine free will, causation, space, matter, and God’s relation to the world. Studying him also reminds us that a historical writer may have ideas that do not fit neatly into the official teachings of the religious community with which he was associated.

important_terms.definition: A philosopher is a person who carefully studies big questions about knowledge, reality, people, and how we should live.
Determinism is the idea that every event, including a choice, follows from earlier causes.
A polemic is a written argument made to defend one side and challenge another side, often in a religious disagreement.
Neoplatonism is a way of thinking that explains the world as flowing from a highest divine source.

summaries.example: Suppose a person chooses whether to study for an exam. Abner would say the decision results from causes such as desires, imagination, past learning, surroundings, and other events. The person may experience deliberation, but Abner denies that the final choice is uncaused. He compares the general capacity to take different forms with wax to the particular shape wax has at a given moment: the capacity exists, but causes determine its actual state.
summaries.summary: Abner of Burgos, also known as Alfonso of Valladolid, was a major medieval philosopher from Castile. During the first part of his career he participated in Jewish Aristotelian philosophy, with links to Maimonidean and Averroist approaches. After years of hesitation, including experiences he described as dreams, he converted to Christianity around 1320 or 1321. His later writings attempted to persuade Jewish readers of Christianity, while also criticizing traditional Judaism and philosophical interpretations of Judaism. These texts are important because their religious polemics contain substantial philosophical argument. Abner developed a radical Neoplatonic account of Christianity. He argued that divine reality is present in the world in degrees and interpreted the Incarnation as the highest human manifestation of this divine essence, rather than simply repeating the standard theological account. His treatment of the Trinity was likewise distinctive and, according to the entry, differed from official Catholic doctrine of his period. Abner also defended a strong form of determinism. He held that will in general has the capacity to take opposing directions, but every particular act of willing is fixed by its causes. This view was intended to reconcile divine foreknowledge with the order of nature, though it raises questions about commandments, reward, and punishment. In natural philosophy, Abner challenged Aristotelian accounts of matter, place, motion, and the void. Much of his scientific work is lost, so scholars reconstruct it from surviving texts and reports. His most important later philosophical influence was on Hasdai Crescas, whose work transmitted several Abnerian themes into later Western philosophy.
key_ideas: Abner began as a Jewish Aristotelian philosopher associated with Maimonidean and Averroist currents, then converted to Christianity after a long period of uncertainty.
His polemical writings presented debates between Christian and Jewish positions, but his arguments also developed original philosophical views.
He claimed that the diversity of the world required a distinction within divine reality and offered a nonstandard account of the Trinity and Incarnation.
His determinism distinguishes the general capacity for willing from particular choices, which he held to be caused.
He criticized Aristotle’s account of place and natural motion, treating dimension as space that can exist independently of bodies and explaining motion through interacting forces.
His direct philosophical influence was chiefly within Jewish philosophy, especially through Hasdai Crescas; his religious arguments did not simply represent official Catholic doctrine.
summaries.why_it_matters: Abner’s importance lies less in a single doctrine than in the way his work links several fields. His religious arguments became part of medieval Jewish-Christian controversy, while his philosophical positions continued to matter within Jewish thought. The entry presents him as an early critic of Aristotelian science and as a source for Crescas’s discussions of determinism, divine attributes, and nature. His case also illustrates why historical interpretation requires care: surviving works, disputed biographical reports, polemical aims, and differences from official theology all affect how his ideas should be understood.

important_terms.definition: Determinism is the thesis that every event is fixed by prior causes and the laws or order of the world; Abner applied it to individual acts of will.
Aristotelianism is a philosophical tradition based on Aristotle, including theories of nature, motion, matter, place, and causation.
Neoplatonism explains reality as proceeding from a transcendent divine source through levels or expressions of being.
The Trinity is the Christian doctrine of one God understood through three persons; Abner gave it a distinctive philosophical interpretation.
Incarnation is the doctrine that divinity is present in human form; Abner interpreted Jesus as the highest manifestation of a divine essence present throughout the world.
A polemical work is an argumentative text written to defend a position and answer an opponent, especially in a religious controversy.
Prime matter is the underlying material principle discussed in Aristotelian philosophy; Abner connected it with a body stripped of ordinary forms and qualities.
Causation is the relation by which events or conditions bring about other events or conditions.

summaries.example: Think about a phone notification. You may decide to check it, but your decision could be influenced by the sound, your curiosity, past habits, and what you were doing already. Abner’s determinism says that a choice works this way on a much larger scale: every choice has causes, even if the person feels free while making it.
summaries.summary: Abner of Burgos was a philosopher, rabbi, and writer in medieval Spain. He was born around 1260 in or near Burgos and first belonged to Jewish philosophical circles influenced by Aristotle, Maimonides, and Averroes. After a long period of uncertainty, he converted to Christianity around 1320 or 1321 and became known as Alfonso of Valladolid. Much of his later writing tried to persuade Jews to accept Christianity. His books often take the form of debates between a Christian speaker and a Jewish opponent. The opponent does not always convert, which makes the dialogue more complex than a simple story of victory. Abner’s religious arguments included unusual philosophical explanations of the Trinity and Incarnation. He held that divine essence is present in the world in different degrees and that Jesus represented the highest degree available to a human being. The entry notes that these views were not the same as the official Catholic doctrine of his period. Abner also argued for determinism. He separated the general ability to choose between alternatives from particular choices made at particular times. Those actual choices, he said, are determined by causes. He thought commandments, rewards, and punishments could still influence people because they become causes that guide behavior. Abner also criticized parts of Aristotelian science, including Aristotle’s accounts of place and natural motion. Some of his scientific writings have been lost, so scholars use surviving passages and reports from others. His strongest later philosophical influence was on Hasdai Crescas, who used some of Abner’s ideas in his own work.
key_ideas: Abner lived in medieval Castile and first worked as a Jewish rabbi, teacher, and philosopher before converting to Christianity.
His main surviving writings include religious debates, but they also discuss science, free will, causation, and the nature of God.
He believed that divine reality is present throughout the world in different degrees and used this idea to explain the Trinity and Incarnation.
He rejected ordinary free will: particular choices are determined by their causes, although people still experience choosing.
He questioned Aristotle’s explanations of space and motion, arguing that motion comes from interacting forces rather than a body being drawn toward a special natural place.
His ideas strongly affected Hasdai Crescas and helped shape later Jewish philosophical discussions.
summaries.why_it_matters: Abner matters because he shows how intellectual life in medieval Spain connected religious communities, philosophy, and natural science. His arguments entered debates about Christianity and Judaism, but his lasting philosophical influence came mainly through Jewish thinkers. His determinism encouraged later discussions about free will, while his criticisms of Aristotle contributed to changing ideas about nature and motion. Studying him also teaches us to read historical arguments in context: a polemical writer may be trying to persuade an audience, and a personal interpretation may differ from an institution’s official position.

important_terms.definition: A philosopher studies basic questions about reality, knowledge, God, nature, and human action by using careful reasoning.
Determinism is the view that events, including human decisions, are fixed by causes that come before them.
Aristotelian philosophy is a tradition based on Aristotle’s ideas about nature, motion, matter, and explanation.
Neoplatonism is a tradition that sees the many things in the world as connected to, or flowing from, a highest divine source.
The Incarnation is the Christian belief that God is present in human form; Abner explained it in his own distinctive way.
A polemical text argues for one side in a serious disagreement and answers the opposing side.
